prompt: Which best describes cloud computing?
explanation: Cloud computing means renting computing resources (servers, storage, databases, software) over the internet and paying per use, instead of owning the hardware.

options.text: Buying and running your own servers on-site
Renting computing resources over the internet and paying for what you use
A programming language for the web
Storing files only on your local hard drive

prompt: In the shared responsibility model, which items are ALWAYS the customer's responsibility, regardless of service model? Select all that apply.
explanation: Data, identities/accounts, and access management are always the customer's responsibility. The provider secures the physical datacenter and underlying infrastructure.

options.text: Your data
Your accounts and identities
Managing who has access
Physical security of the datacenter

prompt: The service model where you use finished software and manage almost nothing (like Microsoft 365) is abbreviated ____.
explanation: SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers finished software over the web; the provider runs everything and you manage only your data and users.

prompt: Order these from the MOST you manage yourself to the LEAST.
explanation: On-premises means you manage everything; IaaS you manage the OS and up; PaaS you manage the app and data; SaaS you manage almost nothing.

prompt: Match each deployment term to its description.
explanation: Public is shared; private is dedicated to one organization; hybrid connects public and private; multicloud uses more than one provider.

pairs.right: Shared provider datacenters open to everyone
Cloud infrastructure dedicated to one organization
Public and private connected together
Using more than one cloud provider

prompt: What is an Azure subscription?
explanation: A subscription is a billing and management boundary. Resources are created inside it and their usage is billed to it; you can have several (e.g., dev and production).

options.text: A programming language used in Azure
A billing and management boundary that resources are created inside
A single virtual machine
The web GUI for managing Azure

prompt: Which of these are ways to interact with Azure? Select all that apply.
explanation: All four are valid ways to work with Azure. They ultimately call the same Azure REST API.

options.text: The Azure portal (web GUI)
The Azure CLI (az)
Azure PowerShell (Az module)
Cloud Shell

prompt: The Azure CLI command that signs you in is `az ____`.
explanation: `az login` opens a browser to authenticate; then `az account show` displays your active subscription.

prompt: Order the Azure hierarchy from broadest to most specific.
explanation: Identity and billing flow account → subscription → resource group → resource.

prompt: Match each tool or term to what it is.
explanation: The portal is the GUI; the CLI is command-line (az); Cloud Shell is a ready-to-use browser shell; a tenant is your Microsoft Entra directory.

pairs.right: Web GUI for exploring and managing Azure
Command-line tool whose commands start with az
A signed-in shell built into the browser
Your organization's directory of users and groups

prompt: What does an availability zone protect against?
explanation: Availability zones are physically separate locations within a region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking, so one zone failing doesn't take the others down.

options.text: A single-datacenter (zone-level) failure within a region
A bug in your application code
Running out of subscription credit
A slow internet connection at the user's home

prompt: Which factors should guide your choice of region? Select all that apply.
explanation: All four matter: proximity/latency, service availability, price differences, and where data must legally reside.

options.text: Latency / proximity to your users
Whether the services and sizes you need are available there
Price (it can vary by region)
Compliance / data-residency requirements

prompt: Two regions in the same geography that some services use for disaster recovery are called a region ____.
explanation: A region pair is two regions in a geography used by some services to replicate for disaster recovery. Not every region has a pair.

prompt: Order these from the SMALLEST unit to the LARGEST.
explanation: Datacenters make up a region; a geography contains one or more regions and preserves data-residency boundaries.

prompt: Match each infrastructure term to its meaning.
explanation: Regions are groups of datacenters; zones are independent locations within a region; geographies preserve residency; sovereign clouds are isolated instances.

pairs.right: A set of nearby datacenters you deploy into
A physically separate, independently powered location in a region
A data-residency and compliance boundary
An isolated Azure instance such as Azure Government

prompt: What is Azure Resource Manager (ARM)?
explanation: ARM is Azure's control plane. Requests from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs, and REST API all go through it for consistent authentication, RBAC, policy, and routing.

options.text: A type of virtual machine
The deployment and management control plane every request goes through
A billing report
A programming language

prompt: Which statements about resource groups are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: A resource lives in exactly one group; deleting the group deletes its contents; the group's location only stores metadata, so it can hold resources from other regions. Groups can be deleted.

options.text: A resource belongs to exactly one resource group at a time
Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside it
A resource group can contain resources from other regions
Resource groups can never be deleted once created

prompt: Name/value labels you attach to resources to organize them and report on cost are called ____.
explanation: Tags are name/value pairs used to organize, filter, and report on resources (especially cost). They are not inherited by default.

prompt: Order the management hierarchy from broadest to most specific.
explanation: Governance flows management group → subscription → resource group → resource.

prompt: Match each term to its role.
explanation: Management groups govern many subscriptions; resource groups contain resources; ARM is the control plane; tags label resources.

pairs.right: Applies governance across many subscriptions
Logical container for related resources
The control plane for all management requests
A label for organizing and cost reporting

prompt: Which service is the fully managed (PaaS) way to host a web app or API?
explanation: App Service is PaaS web hosting: you deploy code or a container and Azure runs, patches, and scales the platform for you.

options.text: Azure Virtual Machine
Azure App Service
Azure Kubernetes Service
Azure Storage

prompt: Which statements about Azure compute are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: VMs give control with OS upkeep; Functions scale to zero and bill per run; AKS is managed Kubernetes. App Service is PaaS — Azure patches the OS, not you.

options.text: A Virtual Machine (IaaS) gives the most control but you maintain the OS
Azure Functions can scale to zero and bill per execution
AKS is managed Kubernetes for complex orchestration
App Service requires you to patch the operating system yourself

prompt: The serverless, event-driven Azure compute service that runs small pieces of code is Azure ____.
explanation: Azure Functions runs event-driven code (HTTP, timer, queue, blob triggers) and, on the Consumption plan, scales to zero and bills per execution.

prompt: Order these from the MOST infrastructure you manage to the LEAST.
explanation: A VM (IaaS) has you manage the OS and up; App Service (PaaS) manages the platform; Functions (serverless) has you supply only code.

prompt: Match each compute service to its description.
explanation: VM = IaaS; App Service = PaaS web hosting; Functions = serverless; AKS = managed Kubernetes.

pairs.right: IaaS computer where you manage the OS
Managed hosting for web apps and APIs
Serverless, event-driven code
Managed Kubernetes for containers

prompt: Which storage service is best for unstructured objects like images, backups, and logs?
explanation: Blob storage is object storage for unstructured data (files, images, video, backups, logs) accessed over HTTP/APIs.

options.text: Blob storage
Azure Files
Queue storage
Table storage

prompt: Which statements about storage redundancy are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: LRS = 3 copies in one datacenter; ZRS = across zones; GRS = plus a secondary region. LRS does NOT protect against a regional outage — you need geo-redundant options for that.

options.text: LRS keeps three copies within a single datacenter
ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in a region
GRS also copies data asynchronously to a secondary region
LRS protects against a full regional outage

prompt: The offline, lowest-cost blob access tier (which must be rehydrated before reading) is the ____ tier.
explanation: The Archive tier is offline and cheapest to store; you must rehydrate a blob (which takes time) before you can read it.

prompt: Order these redundancy options from LEAST resilient to MOST resilient.
explanation: LRS (one datacenter) < ZRS (zones in a region) < GRS (local + secondary region) < GZRS (zonal + secondary region, most resilient).

prompt: Match each storage service to what it provides.
explanation: A storage account provides Blob (objects), Files (shares), Queue (messages), and Table (NoSQL key/value).

pairs.right: Object storage for unstructured data
Managed SMB/NFS file shares
A simple message queue
NoSQL key/value store

prompt: What is an Azure virtual network (VNet)?
explanation: A VNet is your own private, isolated network in a region, divided into subnets, where resources get private IP addresses and communicate.

options.text: A private, isolated network in an Azure region where resources get private IPs
A managed database service
A public DNS provider only
A billing boundary for resources

prompt: Which are valid load-balancing services in Azure? Select all that apply.
explanation: Load Balancer (L4), Application Gateway (regional L7), and Front Door (global L7) distribute traffic. Key Vault is a secrets store, not a load balancer.

options.text: Azure Load Balancer (regional, layer 4)
Application Gateway (regional, layer 7)
Azure Front Door (global, layer 7)
Azure Key Vault

prompt: Allow/deny rules that filter traffic by IP, port, and protocol are configured in a ____ security group.
explanation: A network security group (NSG) filters traffic with allow/deny rules by source/destination IP, port, and protocol, attached to a subnet or NIC.

prompt: Order the path of an inbound request to a web VM from OUTERMOST to the VM.
explanation: Traffic comes from the internet, is distributed by a load balancer, filtered by the NSG, and then reaches the VM.

prompt: Match each connectivity option to its description.
explanation: VPN Gateway is an internet tunnel; ExpressRoute is a private link; Front Door is global L7; Azure DNS hosts your domains.

pairs.right: Encrypted tunnel over the public internet
Private, dedicated connection (not over the internet)
Global layer-7 routing with CDN and WAF
Hosts DNS domains and resolves names

prompt: Which describes authentication (as opposed to authorization)?
explanation: Authentication answers 'who are you?' (proving identity by signing in). Authorization answers 'what may you do?' — that's RBAC.

options.text: Deciding what actions an identity is allowed to perform
Proving who you are, usually by signing in
Billing your usage to a subscription
Encrypting data at rest

prompt: Which statements about Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Entra ID is the renamed Azure AD; RBAC = principal + role + scope, inheriting downward. Entra ID is NOT the same as on-premises AD DS (no OUs/Group Policy/domain join).

options.text: Microsoft Entra ID is the current name for Azure Active Directory
An RBAC role assignment combines a principal, a role, and a scope
Role assignments inherit downward through the hierarchy
Entra ID is identical to on-premises Active Directory Domain Services

prompt: Requiring two or more proofs of identity at sign-in (like a password plus a phone app) is abbreviated ____.
explanation: MFA (multifactor authentication) requires two or more verification factors and blocks the vast majority of password-based attacks.

prompt: Order these built-in roles from LEAST to MOST access.
explanation: Reader can only view; Contributor can manage resources but not grant access; Owner has full access including managing others' access.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
explanation: Owner is full control; Contributor manages resources but not access; Reader is view-only; least privilege grants the minimum necessary.

pairs.right: Full access including managing others' access
Manage resources but not grant access to others
View resources only
Grant only the minimum access needed

prompt: You shut a VM down from inside its operating system. What happens to compute billing?
explanation: An in-OS shutdown leaves the VM allocated, so compute keeps billing. Only deallocating (portal Stop or `az vm deallocate`) releases the compute.

options.text: Compute billing stops immediately
You keep paying for compute because the VM is still allocated
The VM and its disks are permanently deleted
The subscription is cancelled

prompt: Which statements about Azure VMs are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: You pick image and size; SSH keys beat passwords; disks cost while deallocated. Exposing SSH/RDP to the entire internet is a security risk to avoid.

options.text: You choose an image (OS) and a size (CPU/memory) when creating one
SSH keys are more secure than passwords for Linux VMs
Managed disks are billed even while the VM is deallocated
Exposing SSH/RDP to the whole internet is a recommended default

prompt: Releasing a VM's compute so you stop paying for its vCPUs (while keeping the disks) is called ____.
explanation: Deallocating releases the compute so you stop paying for vCPUs; disks and static IPs still cost until you delete them.

prompt: Order the typical lifecycle of a learning VM.
explanation: Create, connect and use, deallocate to pause billing, then delete the resource group to remove everything.

prompt: Match each VM concept to its meaning.
explanation: Image = the OS template; size = CPU/memory; managed disk = the VM's storage; SSH = remote connection for Linux.

pairs.right: The OS/software template a VM starts from
The VM's CPU and memory configuration
An Azure-managed virtual disk backing the VM
How you connect to a Linux VM

prompt: What is the relationship between an App Service plan and a web app?
explanation: The App Service plan provides the compute (region, OS, size, tier); web apps run inside it, and multiple apps can share one plan.

options.text: They are two names for the same thing
The plan is the compute; the web app runs inside it, and several apps can share a plan
The web app is the compute; the plan runs inside the app
A plan can hold only one web app, ever

prompt: Which statements about App Service are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Scale up = bigger, scale out = more instances; autoscale/slots need Standard+; managed certificates give free TLS. App Service is PaaS, so Azure patches the OS.

options.text: Scaling up means moving to a bigger plan; scaling out means more instances
Autoscale and deployment slots require Standard tier or higher
A managed certificate can provide free HTTPS on a custom domain
You must patch the underlying OS yourself

prompt: A live copy of a web app (like 'staging') that you can swap into production for a zero-downtime release is a deployment ____.
explanation: Deployment slots (Standard+) let you deploy and test in staging, then swap into production near-instantly, with an easy swap-back to roll back.

prompt: Order the steps of a zero-downtime release using slots.
explanation: Deploy to staging, test there, then swap into production; if there's a problem, swap back to roll back.

items.text: Deploy the new version to the staging slot

prompt: Match each App Service term to its meaning.
explanation: The plan is the compute; scale up = bigger; scale out = more instances; a slot is a swappable copy.

pairs.right: The compute apps run on
Move to a bigger plan
Run more instances
A swappable live copy like staging

prompt: What is a trigger in Azure Functions?
explanation: Every function has exactly one trigger — the event (HTTP request, timer, queue message, new blob, etc.) that starts it. Bindings then connect it to data.

options.text: The single event that starts a function running
A way to store secrets
The billing plan for the function app
A network security rule

prompt: Which statements about the Consumption plan are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Consumption scales to zero, bills per run, and can cold-start with a time limit. Long-running, always-on work is a poor fit — use Premium/Dedicated or another service.

options.text: It scales automatically, including to zero when idle
You pay per execution
It can have cold starts and a maximum execution time
It's ideal for long-running, always-on processes

prompt: The short startup delay when a new instance spins up after the function has been idle is called a cold ____.
explanation: A cold start is the startup delay after idle. The Premium plan avoids it by keeping instances pre-warmed.

prompt: Order the flow of a blob-triggered function that writes a result.
explanation: An event (new blob) fires the trigger, the function runs, and an output binding writes the result — with little glue code.

items.text: An output binding writes the result

prompt: Match each Functions concept to its meaning.
explanation: Trigger starts the function; bindings connect to data; Consumption scales to zero; Premium stays warm.

pairs.right: The event that starts a function
A declarative connection to data
Scales to zero, bills per execution
Keeps instances pre-warmed (no cold starts)

prompt: What is a Shared Access Signature (SAS)?
explanation: A SAS is a time-limited, scoped token (usually in a URL) granting specific permissions. A user-delegation SAS, signed with Entra ID credentials, is preferred over key-based SAS.

options.text: A permanent master key for the whole storage account
A time-limited, scoped token that grants specific permissions to storage data
A type of blob access tier
A network security group rule

prompt: Which are good security practices for Blob storage? Select all that apply.
explanation: Prefer Entra ID/RBAC; keep SAS scoped and short; prefer user-delegation SAS. Never embed account keys in app code — a leak exposes the whole account.

options.text: Prefer Microsoft Entra ID + RBAC for access
Keep SAS tokens narrowly scoped and short-lived
Use a user-delegation SAS instead of an account-key SAS when possible
Embed account keys directly in application code

prompt: Rules that automatically move blobs between tiers or delete them based on age are called ____ management.
explanation: Lifecycle management rules auto-transition blobs between tiers (e.g., to cool/archive) or delete them by age, reducing cost without manual work.

prompt: Order the steps to share a single blob with a read-only SAS.
explanation: Scope permissions to read, set a short expiry, generate the SAS, then share the URL — least privilege and minimal exposure.

prompt: Match each authorization method or feature to its description.
explanation: Account keys are all-powerful (avoid in apps); SAS is scoped/temporary; Entra ID + RBAC is most secure; static website hosting serves files from $web.

pairs.right: Master key for the whole account (avoid in apps)
Time-limited, scoped access token
Most secure, manageable access
Serves files from the $web container

prompt: Which option is a fully managed (PaaS) relational database for new apps?
explanation: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed PaaS relational database (SQL Server engine) where Azure handles patching, backups, and high availability.

options.text: SQL Server on an Azure VM
Azure SQL Database
Azure Blob storage
Azure Cosmos DB

prompt: Which statements about Azure SQL purchasing and options are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: vCore sizes compute and storage separately; serverless can auto-pause; new servers block connections until a firewall rule is added. DTU is a bundled model, not separate sizing.

options.text: vCore lets you size compute and storage independently
The serverless tier can auto-pause when idle
A new SQL server blocks all connections until you add a firewall rule
DTU lets you choose cores and storage completely separately

prompt: The purchasing model Microsoft generally recommends, where you size compute and storage separately, is ____.
explanation: vCore lets you choose compute (cores + memory) and storage independently, supports serverless and Azure Hybrid Benefit, and is generally recommended.

prompt: Order the steps to create and connect to an Azure SQL database.
explanation: Create the server, then the database, allow your client IP through the firewall, and finally connect and query.

items.text: Add a firewall rule for your IP

prompt: Match each option to its description.
explanation: SQL Database is PaaS; Managed Instance is high-compatibility PaaS; SQL on a VM is IaaS; serverless auto-scales and pauses.

pairs.right: Fully managed PaaS database for new apps
Managed instance with near-full SQL Server compatibility
Self-managed database (IaaS)
Auto-scales and auto-pauses compute

prompt: What are Request Units per second (RU/s) in Cosmos DB?
explanation: RU/s is the currency for throughput and cost — a single unit bundles the CPU, memory, and I/O an operation uses. You provision RU/s or use serverless pay-per-request.

options.text: The number of regions your data is replicated to
The currency measuring the throughput/cost of operations
The maximum size of a single item
The number of consistency levels available

prompt: Which statements about Cosmos DB are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Good keys are high-cardinality and even; poor keys cause hot partitions; Session is the default. The partition key is a foundational choice that's hard to change later.

options.text: A good partition key has high cardinality and spreads load evenly
A poor partition key can create a hot partition that gets throttled
Session is the default consistency level
The partition key is trivial to change after the fact

prompt: The default Cosmos DB consistency level, which guarantees you read your own writes within a client session, is ____.
explanation: Session is the default — consistent within a client session (read your own writes) — offering much better latency and availability than Strong.

prompt: Order the five consistency levels from STRONGEST to WEAKEST.
explanation: The spectrum runs Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, Eventual — trading consistency for lower latency and higher availability.

prompt: Match each Cosmos DB concept to its meaning.
explanation: NoSQL is the native API; the partition key distributes data; a hot partition is overloaded; RU/s measures throughput/cost.

pairs.right: The native document API for new apps
Property that distributes data across partitions
Overloaded partition from a poor key choice
Throughput and cost currency

prompt: What does a private endpoint do?
explanation: A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP in your VNet that connects privately (via Private Link) to a PaaS service, keeping traffic off the public internet.

options.text: Gives a PaaS service a private IP inside your VNet so traffic avoids the public internet
Makes a storage account public to everyone
Encrypts a virtual machine's disk
Assigns a role to a user

prompt: Which statements about VNet peering are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Peering privately connects VNets, requires non-overlapping ranges, and is non-transitive. It must be created on both VNets to work.

options.text: It connects two VNets so resources communicate over private IPs
Peered VNets must have non-overlapping address spaces
Peering is non-transitive (A-B and B-C does not connect A and C)
Peering only needs to be created on one of the two VNets

prompt: VNet peering is non-____, meaning peering A-B and B-C does not automatically connect A and C.
explanation: Peering is non-transitive; you must connect A and C directly or use a hub-and-spoke design with routing.

prompt: Order the steps to build and secure a subnet.
explanation: Create the VNet, carve a subnet, create an NSG with rules, then associate the NSG with the subnet.

items.text: Associate the NSG with the subnet

prompt: Match each networking concept to its meaning.
explanation: Address space is the VNet's IP range; subnets subdivide it; peering connects VNets; private endpoints give PaaS a private IP.

pairs.right: The private IP range a VNet owns
A subdivision of a VNet grouping resources
Private connectivity between two VNets
A private IP in your VNet for a PaaS service

prompt: What is the main benefit of a managed identity?
explanation: A managed identity is an Entra ID identity for an Azure resource that lets it authenticate to services like Key Vault without any stored credentials to leak.

options.text: It lets an app authenticate to services without any stored credentials
It stores your application's source code
It is a faster type of virtual machine
It encrypts network traffic

prompt: Which statements are true about Key Vault and managed identities? Select all that apply.
explanation: Key Vault holds secrets/keys/certs; system-assigned identities are tied to one resource, user-assigned are reusable; Key Vault references inject secrets at runtime. Non-secret settings belong in App Configuration.

options.text: Key Vault stores secrets, keys, and certificates
A system-assigned identity is tied to one resource; a user-assigned one is reusable
Key Vault references let App Service inject a secret into a setting at runtime
You should store non-secret settings and feature flags in Key Vault

prompt: An automatically managed Entra ID identity for a resource, so it needs no stored password, is called a managed ____.
explanation: A managed identity lets a resource authenticate as itself (system-assigned or user-assigned) with no credentials stored in code or config.

prompt: Order the steps of the secure secret-access pattern.
explanation: Store the secret, give the app an identity, grant that identity least-privilege access to the vault, and the app fetches the secret at runtime — no secret in code.

items.text: Store the secret in Key Vault
Give the app a managed identity
Grant that identity access to the vault
The app reads the secret at runtime

prompt: Match each service or feature to its role.
explanation: Key Vault stores secrets; managed identities remove stored credentials; App Configuration holds non-secret settings; Key Vault references inject secrets into settings.

pairs.right: Secure store for secrets, keys, and certificates
Credential-free authentication for a resource
Centralized non-secret settings and feature flags
A setting that resolves to a vault secret at runtime

prompt: Which best describes metrics compared with logs in Azure Monitor?
explanation: Metrics are lightweight, numeric, near-real-time time-series values (great for dashboards and quick alerts). Logs are richer, structured records stored in Log Analytics and queried with KQL.

options.text: Metrics are numeric, near-real-time time-series values
Metrics are long text records queried with KQL
Metrics can only be viewed once per day
Metrics are the same thing as alerts

prompt: Which statements about Azure Monitor are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: App Insights is APM; logs live in Log Analytics (KQL); alerts trigger action groups. Over-alerting causes alert fatigue — alert only on actionable conditions.

options.text: Application Insights provides application performance monitoring
Logs are stored in a Log Analytics workspace and queried with KQL
An alert rule can use an action group to notify or automate a response
Creating many noisy, low-value alerts is a best practice

prompt: The query language used to analyze logs in a Log Analytics workspace is abbreviated ____.
explanation: KQL (Kusto Query Language) is a pipe-based language used to query logs, power log-based alerts, and build workbooks.

prompt: Order what happens when a monitored condition is breached.
explanation: A signal breaches the condition, the alert rule fires, its action group runs, and it notifies people or automates a response.

items.text: A signal crosses the alert condition
People are notified or a response is automated

prompt: Match each monitoring concept to its meaning.
explanation: Azure Monitor is the umbrella; metrics are numeric; Log Analytics stores logs (KQL); App Insights is APM.

pairs.right: The umbrella platform for telemetry and alerting
A numeric, near-real-time time-series value
Where logs are stored and queried with KQL
Application performance monitoring

prompt: What is Azure Container Registry (ACR)?
explanation: ACR is Azure's private container registry for storing images; it can also build images in the cloud with `az acr build`. Container services pull images from it.

options.text: A private registry for storing (and building) container images
A managed relational database
A load balancer for containers
A monitoring dashboard

prompt: Which statements about container services are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: ACI runs single containers; Container Apps is serverless with scale-to-zero; AKS is managed Kubernetes. AKS has the MOST operational overhead, not the least.

options.text: ACI runs single containers serverlessly, billed per second
Container Apps is serverless and can scale to zero
AKS is managed Kubernetes for full orchestration control
AKS is the simplest option with the least operational overhead

prompt: The serverless platform for containers and microservices that can scale to zero is Azure Container ____.
explanation: Azure Container Apps is a serverless container platform (built on Kubernetes + KEDA) with autoscaling including scale-to-zero, ingress, and revisions.

prompt: Order the steps to run a container on Azure.
explanation: Build the image, push it to a registry like ACR, then deploy it to ACI, Container Apps, or AKS.

items.text: Deploy it to a container service

prompt: Match each service to what it's best for.
explanation: ACI = single containers; Container Apps = serverless microservices; AKS = full Kubernetes; ACR = image storage.

pairs.right: A single container, run and go
Serverless microservices with autoscaling
Full Kubernetes control
Storing container images

prompt: How does Bicep relate to ARM templates?
explanation: Bicep is a domain-specific language that transpiles to ARM JSON. Anything ARM can do, Bicep can express more readably; both deploy through Azure Resource Manager.

options.text: Bicep is a concise language that transpiles to ARM JSON
Bicep replaces Azure Resource Manager entirely
Bicep is a monitoring tool
Bicep and ARM are unrelated products

prompt: Which statements about infrastructure as code are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: IaC is repeatable and reviewable; Bicep is declarative and idempotent; parameters enable reuse. Manual portal edits cause drift — the files should be the source of truth.

options.text: IaC makes environments repeatable and reviewable
Bicep deployments are declarative and idempotent
Parameters let one template serve multiple environments
Editing resources by hand in the portal is the recommended way to avoid drift

prompt: The command that previews exactly what a deployment would change, without changing anything, is `az deployment group ____`.
explanation: `what-if` previews the create/change/delete actions a deployment would make, so you can review the impact before deploying.

prompt: Order the safe deployment workflow for Bicep.
explanation: Author the Bicep, preview changes with what-if, then deploy — especially important for shared or production environments.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
explanation: IaC = infra in files; declarative = describe the end state; idempotent = no duplicates on redeploy; modules = reusable pieces.

pairs.right: Defining infrastructure in version-controlled files
You describe the desired end state
Redeploying converges to the same state without duplicates
A reusable Bicep file called with parameters

prompt: Why is OIDC (workload identity federation) preferred over a service principal secret for pipeline authentication?
explanation: OIDC lets the pipeline prove its identity with a short-lived token and no stored secret — so there's nothing to leak or rotate, unlike a stored client secret.

options.text: It uses a short-lived token with no stored secret to leak or rotate
It makes deployments run faster
It removes the need for any permissions in Azure
It only works for private repositories

prompt: Which statements about CI/CD are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: CI builds/tests changes; Actions and Pipelines are YAML tools; environments support approvals. Prefer OIDC over storing long-lived secrets.

options.text: CI automatically builds and tests every change
GitHub Actions and Azure Pipelines are both YAML-based CI/CD tools
Environments can require a manual approval before deploying to production
Storing long-lived secrets in the repo is the recommended auth method

prompt: In CI/CD, 'CI' stands for continuous ____.
explanation: CI is Continuous Integration — automatically building and testing every change so problems surface immediately.

prompt: Order the steps of a deploy pipeline that uses OIDC.
explanation: A typical workflow checks out code, authenticates to Azure (OIDC), builds and tests, then deploys.

items.text: Log in to Azure with OIDC

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
explanation: CI builds/tests; CD releases; GitHub Actions is a YAML CI/CD tool; OIDC is secretless auth.

pairs.right: Auto build and test on every change
Auto release to an environment (often gated)
YAML CI/CD workflows in a GitHub repo
Secretless pipeline authentication to Azure

prompt: What does Azure Policy do?
explanation: Azure Policy enforces organizational rules on how resources are configured — it can audit, deny non-compliant creates, or remediate. (RBAC governs who can act; Policy governs how resources are configured.)

options.text: Enforces rules on resource configurations (audit, deny, or remediate)
Controls which users can sign in to Azure
Stores application secrets
Load-balances network traffic

prompt: Which are legitimate ways to reduce Azure spend? Select all that apply.
explanation: Right-sizing, reservations/savings plans, and Hybrid Benefit all cut cost. Azure Advisor's recommendations should be used, not ignored.

options.text: Right-size resources and shut down idle ones
Buy reservations or savings plans for steady workloads
Use Azure Hybrid Benefit to reuse existing licenses
Ignore Azure Advisor's cost recommendations

prompt: The resource lock type that lets you read and modify a resource but not delete it is ____.
explanation: A CanNotDelete lock allows reading and modifying but prevents deletion — ideal for protecting critical resources like a production database.

prompt: Order a sensible cost-control workflow.
explanation: Estimate up front, track real spend, set budgets, and receive alerts before you overspend.

items.text: Track actual spend in Cost Management
Set a budget with a threshold
Get alerted as you approach it

prompt: Match each governance tool to its role.
explanation: Policy enforces config rules; locks protect resources; budgets watch spend; management groups scale governance across subscriptions.

pairs.right: Enforces resource configuration rules
Prevents accidental change or deletion
A spending threshold with alerts
Applies policy/RBAC across many subscriptions

prompt: Which phrase best summarizes the Zero Trust model?
explanation: Zero Trust means 'never trust, always verify': verify explicitly, use least-privilege access, and assume breach. Identity — not the network perimeter — is the primary control.

options.text: Trust everything inside the network perimeter
Never trust, always verify
Security is only the provider's job
Disable authentication for speed

prompt: Which statements about Azure security are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Defender for Cloud gives a secure score; Sentinel is SIEM/SOAR; encryption at rest is on by default for many services. Security is shared — configuration and access are the customer's job.

options.text: Defender for Cloud provides a secure score and recommendations
Microsoft Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM/SOAR
Data at rest is encrypted by default for many Azure services
In the cloud, security is entirely the provider's responsibility

prompt: Microsoft Defender for Cloud summarizes how well you follow best practices as a single percentage called the ____ score.
explanation: The secure score is a single percentage summarizing your security posture, with prioritized recommendations to raise it.

prompt: Order the steps to improve your secure score.
explanation: Open the secure score, review recommendations, remediate the highest-impact ones first, and the score improves as you comply.

items.text: Open Defender for Cloud's Secure Score
Watch the score rise as you comply

prompt: Match each security concept to its meaning.
explanation: Defender for Cloud manages posture; Sentinel is SIEM/SOAR; encryption at rest protects stored data; PIM grants admin access just-in-time.

pairs.right: Security posture management and workload protection
Cloud-native SIEM and SOAR
Protecting stored data
Just-in-time elevation of admin roles

prompt: How does the composite SLA of two services that depend on each other in series compare with each service alone?
explanation: In series, SLAs multiply into a lower composite (e.g., 99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%). Parallel redundancy is what raises effective availability.

options.text: It is higher than either service
It is lower, because the SLAs multiply together
It is exactly the same as each service
SLAs cannot be combined at all

prompt: Which statements about reliability and scaling are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: Zones protect against datacenter outages; scaling out adds instances; autoscale reacts to metrics/schedules. Scaling up has a ceiling — scale out for elasticity and resilience.

options.text: Availability zones protect against a whole-datacenter outage
Scaling out adds more instances behind a load balancer
Autoscale can add/remove instances based on metrics or a schedule
Scaling up has no practical upper limit

prompt: The measure of how much data loss you can tolerate (how far back your last good copy is) is abbreviated ____.
explanation: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is tolerable data loss; RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is tolerable downtime. Design backup/DR to meet both.

prompt: Order these from LEAST to MOST resilient.
explanation: Resilience grows from a single instance, to an availability set (rack/maintenance protection), to zones (datacenter outage), to multiple regions (regional disaster).

prompt: Match each reliability concept to its meaning.
explanation: An SLA is the uptime commitment; availability sets protect within a datacenter; zones protect across datacenters; RTO is tolerable downtime.

pairs.right: The provider's uptime commitment for a service
VMs spread across fault/update domains in one datacenter
VMs spread across separate datacenters in a region
How quickly you must be back online

prompt: What is the difference between the Well-Architected Framework (WAF) and the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF)?
explanation: WAF guides the design of a single workload (via the five pillars); CAF guides the organization's overall cloud journey — strategy, readiness (landing zones), governance, and management.

options.text: WAF guides an individual workload's design; CAF guides the organization's whole cloud journey
They are two names for the same checklist
WAF is about billing; CAF is about networking
CAF replaces WAF entirely

prompt: Which of these are pillars of the Azure Well-Architected Framework? Select all that apply.
explanation: The five pillars are Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, and Performance Efficiency. 'Marketing Reach' is not one of them.

options.text: Reliability
Security
Cost Optimization
Marketing Reach

prompt: The framework that guides an organization's entire cloud journey (strategy, readiness, governance, management) is the Cloud ____ Framework.
explanation: The Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) guides the whole organizational journey; the Well-Architected Framework guides each individual workload.

prompt: Order the steps of a good architecture process.
explanation: Understand requirements, evaluate against the pillars, make and document deliberate trade-offs, and revisit as needs change.

items.text: Evaluate the design against the five pillars

prompt: Match each Well-Architected pillar to its focus.
explanation: Reliability = availability/recovery; Security = protection; Cost Optimization = value per dollar; Performance Efficiency = effective, scalable resource use.

pairs.right: Staying available and recovering from failure
Protecting data and systems
Getting the most value per dollar
Using resources effectively and scaling to demand

prompt: What is the primary capability provided by Azure Workbooks?

options.text: Deploying virtual machines with declarative ARM templates
Interactive visual reports combining rich text, KQL queries, metrics, and parameters
Managing database user logins and table indexes
Automatic failover of paired storage accounts

explanation: Azure Workbooks combine metrics, log queries (KQL), text, and parameters into customizable interactive observability and operational reports.

prompt: Which destinations can Diagnostic Settings stream resource logs and metrics to? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Log Analytics workspace
Azure Storage Account for long-term archiving
Azure Event Hubs for real-time streaming to third-party SIEMs
On-premises tape drives directly

explanation: Diagnostic settings route telemetry to Log Analytics (for querying), Storage accounts (for archive retention), Event Hubs (for external streaming), or partner solutions.

prompt: The operational problem caused by receiving too many false or non-actionable notifications is called alert ____.
explanation: Alert fatigue occurs when operators become desensitized to frequent, low-priority notifications, potentially overlooking critical production outages.

prompt: Order the steps of a typical KQL log query from initial source selection to visual aggregation.

items.text: Filter records with where (e.g. where Success == false)
Aggregate counts with summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)

explanation: KQL pipelines flow from table input -> filtering -> aggregation -> rendering.

prompt: Match each Application Insights telemetry concept to its description.

pairs.right: Near real-time 1-second latency health and request stream
Visual topology of app components and outbound dependencies
End-to-end distributed trace for an individual user request
Machine-learning proactive alerts for abnormal failure spikes

explanation: Live Metrics stream immediately; Application Map visualizes architecture; Transaction Diagnostics traces requests end-to-end; Smart Detection surfaces anomalies automatically.

prompt: In Azure Container Apps, what role does KEDA play?

options.text: Compiling source code into Docker container images
Event-driven horizontal autoscaling based on queue depth, HTTP requests, or CPU/memory
Encrypting managed disks at rest with customer keys
Routing DNS queries across geographic regions

explanation: KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) provides rich scaling triggers based on events (like Service Bus queue depth or Kafka topics), including scaling down to zero instances.

prompt: Which statements are true when comparing Kubenet vs Azure CNI networking in AKS? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Kubenet conserves VNet IP address space by assigning pod IPs from a private internal overlay
Azure CNI assigns every pod an IP address directly from the subnet, enabling direct VNet communication
Azure CNI requires careful subnet IP sizing before cluster deployment
Kubenet requires all nodes to be run on bare-metal physical servers only

explanation: Kubenet uses internal NAT/masquerading to conserve VNet IPs, whereas Azure CNI allocates full VNet IPs directly to pods for native network performance.

prompt: The automated security scanner in Microsoft Defender for Cloud that discovers image CVEs inside Azure Container Registry is called vulnerability ____.
explanation: ACR vulnerability scanning (integrated with Defender for Cloud) scans container images pushed to registries to detect known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs).

prompt: Order the steps to build, push, and store an image in Azure Container Registry using the Azure CLI.

items.text: Create an ACR registry with az acr create
Authenticate local Docker client using az acr login
Tag the local image with the registry login server name
Push the image to the registry with docker push or az acr build

explanation: You first provision ACR, authenticate, tag the image with the ACR endpoint, and push the image.

prompt: Match each Azure container service to its primary architectural sweet spot.

pairs.right: Fast, isolated single-container tasks and batch runs
Serverless microservices with built-in ingress and scale-to-zero
Full orchestration control for complex distributed container workloads
Private storage and scanning for OCI container images

explanation: ACI is best for simple fast containers, ACA for serverless microservices, AKS for full Kubernetes orchestration, and ACR for storing images.
